cues.en: One of my earliest memories
cues.zh: 最早的一段记忆

cues.en: is of trying to wake up one of my relatives and not being able to.
cues.zh: 是试图叫醒我的一个亲戚，却怎么也唤不醒。

cues.en: And I was just a little kid, so I didn't really understand why. But as I got older, I realized we had drug addiction in my family, including later cocaine addiction.
cues.zh: 那时我还小，不太明白为什么。但长大后我才意识到，我们家有毒品成瘾问题，后来还包括可卡因成瘾。

cues.en: I've been thinking about it a lot lately, partly because it's now exactly a hundred years since drugs were first banned in The United States and Britain, and we then imposed that on the rest of the world. It's a century since we made this really fateful decision
cues.zh: 最近我一直在思考这件事，部分原因是美国和中国首次禁毒至今正好一百年，之后我们又把这套强加给了世界其他地方。整整一个世纪前，我们做出了这个极其重大的决定

cues.en: to take addicts
cues.zh: 把成瘾者

cues.en: and punish them and make them suffer because we believed that would deter them, it would give them an incentive to stop.
cues.zh: 抓起来惩罚他们、让他们受苦，因为我们相信这样能震慑他们，给他们停下来的动力。

cues.en: And a few years ago, I was looking at some of the addicts in my life who I love and trying to figure out if there was some way to help them,
cues.zh: 几年前，我看着身边一些我深爱的成瘾者，想找出办法帮帮他们，

cues.en: And I realized there were loads of incredibly basic questions I just didn't know the answer to, like, what really causes addiction?
cues.zh: 然后我意识到，有很多极其基本的问题我根本答不上来，比如，成瘾的真正原因是什么？

cues.en: Why do we carry on with this approach that doesn't seem to be working? And is there a better way out there that we could try instead? I read loads of stuff about it, and I couldn't really find the answers I was looking for. So I thought, okay, I'll go and sit with different people around the world who lived this and studied this and talk to them and see if I can learn from them. I didn't realize I would end up going over 30 miles at the start, but I ended up going and meeting loads of different people, from a transgender crack dealer in Brownsville, Brooklyn to a scientist who spends a lot of time feeding hallucinogens to mongooses to see if they like them. It
cues.zh: 为什么我们还在沿用这套似乎并不奏效的做法？有没有更好的替代方案可以尝试？我读了很多相关资料，却找不到想要的答案。于是我想，好吧，我去世界各地和经历过、研究过这些的人坐下来聊聊，看看能不能从他们身上学到什么。我没想到一开始只打算走三十多英里，结果却见了各种各样的人，从布鲁克林布朗斯维尔的跨性别快克贩子，到一位花大量时间给猫鼬喂致幻剂、看它们喜不喜欢的科学家。结果

cues.en: turns out they do, but only in very specific circumstances.
cues.zh: 它们确实喜欢，但只在非常特定的情况下。

cues.en: To to the only country that's ever decriminalized all drugs from cannabis to crack, Portugal.
cues.zh: 去往唯一一个将所有毒品——从大麻到强效可卡因——都非罪化的国家，葡萄牙。

cues.en: And the thing I realized that really blew my mind is almost
cues.zh: 我意识到一件让我大为震惊的事，那就是几乎

cues.en: everything we think we know about addiction is wrong.
cues.zh: 我们对成瘾自以为知的一切都是错的。

cues.en: And if we start to absorb the new evidence about addiction, I think we're going to have to change a lot more than our drug policies.
cues.zh: 如果我们开始吸收关于成瘾的新证据，我认为我们要改变的将远不止毒品政策。

cues.en: But let's start with what we think we know, what I thought I know. Right? Let's think about this middle row here. Right?
cues.zh: 但让我们从我们自以为知道的、我自以为知道的东西开始。对吧？让我们看看中间这一排。对吧？

cues.en: Imagine all of you, for twenty days now, went off and used heroin three times a day. Some of you look a little bit more enthusiastic than others at this prospect.
cues.zh: 想象你们所有人，到现在二十天了，每天都去一天用三次海洛因。你们中有些人看起来对这个设想比别人更热情一点。

cues.en: Don't worry, it's just a thought experiment. Imagine you did that. Right? What would happen? Now, we have a story about what would happen that we've been told for a century.
cues.zh: 别担心，这只是个思想实验。想象你真的这么做了。对吧？会发生什么？现在，关于会发生什么，有一个流传了一个世纪的说法。

cues.en: We think because there are chemical hooks in heroin,
cues.zh: 我们认为因为海洛因里含有化学钩子，

cues.en: as you took it for a while, your body would become dependent on those hooks, you'd start to physically need them, and at the end of those twenty days, you'd all be heroin addicts. Right? That's what I thought. First thing that alerted me to the fact,
cues.zh: 你吸食一段时间后，你的身体就会依赖这些钩子，你会开始生理上需要它们，而在这二十天结束时，你们全都会成为海洛因成瘾者。对吧？我当时就是这么想的。第一件让我警觉到事实——

cues.en: something not right with this story. It's what it was explained to me. If I step out of this TED Talk today and I get hit by a car and I break my hip,
cues.zh: 这个说法有问题的事，是别人向我解释的方式。如果我今天走出这个TED演讲，被车撞了，摔断了髋骨，

cues.en: I'll be taken to hospital and I'll be given loads of diamorphine.
cues.zh: 我会被送到医院，然后被注射大量二乙酰吗啡。

cues.en: Diamorphine
cues.zh: 二乙酰吗啡

cues.en: is heroin. It's actually much better heroin than you're ever going to buy on the streets, because the stuff you buy from a drug dealer is contaminated. Actually, very little of it is heroin, whereas the stuff you get from the doctor is medically pure. And you'll be given it for quite a long period of time. There are loads of people in this room may not realize that you've taken quite a lot of heroin. Right? And
cues.zh: 就是海洛因。实际上，它比你在大街上能买到的海洛因要好得多，因为从毒贩那里买的东西受到了污染。实际上，其中几乎没有海洛因，而从医生那里得到的是医学上纯净的。而且你会被给予相当长的一段时间。这个房间里的许多人可能没有意识到你已经吸食了相当多的海洛因。对吧？而且

cues.en: anyone watching this anywhere in the world, this is happening.
cues.zh: 世界上任何地方观看此节目的人，这种情况都在发生。

cues.en: And if what we believe about addiction is right, those people are exposed to all those chemical hooks,
cues.zh: 如果我们对成瘾的看法是正确的，那些人就接触到了所有那些化学钩子，

cues.en: what should happen?
cues.zh: 应该会发生什么？

cues.en: They should become addicts.
cues.zh: 他们应该成为瘾君子。

cues.en: This has been studied really carefully.
cues.zh: 这已经被非常仔细地研究过了。

cues.en: It doesn't happen. You would have noticed if your grandmother had a hip replacement, she didn't come out as a junkie.
cues.zh: 这并没有发生。如果你祖母做了髋关节置换手术，你会注意到她没有变成瘾君子。

cues.en: And when I learned this, it just seemed so weird to me. So contrary to everything I'd been told, everything I thought I knew, I just thought it couldn't be right, until I went and met a man called Bruce Alexander, who's a professor of psychology in Vancouver,
cues.zh: 当我了解到这一点时，我觉得太奇怪了。与我被告知的一切、我以为我知道的一切都如此相反，我只是觉得这不可能对，直到我去见了一个叫Bruce Alexander的人，他是温哥华的心理学教授，

cues.en: who carried out an incredible experiment that I think really helps us to understand this issue.
cues.zh: 他进行了一项令人难以置信的实验，我认为这真的有助于我们理解这个问题。

cues.en: Professor Alexander explained to me, The idea of addiction we've all got in our heads, that story,
cues.zh: Alexander教授向我解释说，我们脑中关于成瘾的观念，那个故事，

cues.en: comes partly from a series of experiments that were done earlier in the twentieth century. They're really simple experiments. You can do them tonight when you go home if you feel a little bit sadistic.
cues.zh: 部分来自二十世纪早期进行的一系列实验。它们是非常简单的实验。如果你觉得有点虐待狂倾向，今晚回家就可以做。

cues.en: You get a rat and you put it in a cage. You give it two water bottles. One is just water, and the other is water laced with either heroin or cocaine.
cues.zh: 你抓一只老鼠，把它放进笼子里，给它两个水瓶。一个装的是普通水，另一个掺了海洛因或可卡因。

cues.en: If you do that, the rat will almost always prefer the drug water
cues.zh: 这样一来，老鼠几乎总是更喜欢那瓶药水，

cues.en: and almost always kill itself quite quickly.
cues.zh: 而且几乎总是很快就把自己弄死了。

cues.en: So there you go, right? That's how we think it works. In the seventies, professor Alexander comes along and he looks at this experiment, and he noticed something. He said, ah, we're putting the rat in an empty cage.
cues.zh: 你看，对吧？我们就是这么理解成瘾的。到了七十年代，Alexander教授出现了，他研究了这个实验，注意到了一个问题。他说，啊，我们把老鼠关进了一个空笼子。

cues.en: It's got nothing to do except use these drugs. Let's try something a bit different. So professor Alexander built a cage that he called Rat Park, which is basically heaven for rats. Right? They've got loads of cheese, they've got loads of colored balls, they've got loads of tunnels.
cues.zh: 它除了嗑药无事可做。咱们换个花样试试。于是Alexander教授造了一个笼子，叫它“老鼠乐园”，基本上就是老鼠的天堂。对吧？里面有吃不完的奶酪、数不清的彩色球、还有一大堆隧道。

cues.en: Crucially,
cues.zh: 关键在于，

cues.en: they've got loads of friends, they can have loads of sex,
cues.zh: 它们有大量的伙伴，可以尽情交配，

cues.en: and they've got both the water bottles, the normal water and the drugged water.
cues.zh: 而且两个水瓶都在，普通水和药水都有。

cues.en: But here's the fascinating thing.
cues.zh: 但有趣的是，

cues.en: In Rat Park,
cues.zh: 在老鼠乐园里，

cues.en: they don't like the drugged water.
cues.zh: 它们不喜欢那瓶药水。

cues.en: They almost never use it,
cues.zh: 它们几乎从不碰它，

cues.en: none of them ever use it compulsively,
cues.zh: 没有一只是强迫性地去喝，

cues.en: none of them ever overdose. You go from almost a hundred percent overdose when they're isolated
cues.zh: 也没有一只过量。从隔离时几乎百分之百的过量率，

cues.en: to zero percent overdose when they have happy and connected lives. Now, when he first saw this, professor Alexander thought, you know, maybe this is just a thing about rats. They're quite different to us. You know, maybe not as different as we'd like, but you know.
cues.zh: 变成了生活快乐、有社交联系时的百分之零。Alexander教授第一次看到这个结果时想，你知道，也许这只是老鼠的特性，它们和我们差别很大。也许没有我们以为的那么大，但你知道……

cues.en: But fortunately, there was a human experiment into the exact same principle happening at the exact same time. It was called the Vietnam War.
cues.zh: 但幸运的是，几乎在同一时间，有人类实验在验证完全相同的原理。那就是越南战争。

cues.en: In Vietnam,
cues.zh: 在越南，

cues.en: twenty percent of all American troops were using loads of heroin.
cues.zh: 百分之二十的美军士兵大量使用海洛因。

cues.en: And if you look at the news reports from the time, they were really worried because they thought, my god, we're going to have hundreds of thousands of junkies on the streets of The United States when the war ends. It made total sense. Now, those soldiers who were using loads of heroin were followed home. The archives of general psychiatry did a really detailed study, and what happened to them?
cues.zh: 如果你看当时的新闻报道，他们非常担心，因为他们觉得，天哪，战争结束后，美国街头会有几十万个瘾君子。这完全说得通。后来，那些大量使用海洛因的士兵被跟踪调查回了家。《普通精神病学档案》做了一项非常详细的研究，他们后来怎么样了？

cues.en: It turns out they didn't go to rehab.
cues.zh: 结果他们没有去戒毒所。

cues.en: They didn't go into withdrawal.
cues.zh: 他们没有出现戒断反应。

cues.en: Ninety five percent of them
cues.zh: 其中百分之九十五的人

cues.en: just stopped. Now, if you believe the story about chemical hooks, that makes absolutely no sense. But professor Alexander began to think there might be a different story about addiction. He said, what if addiction isn't about your chemical hooks?
cues.zh: 就这么停了。如果你相信关于化学成瘾的这套说法，这完全说不通。但Alexander教授开始思考，关于成瘾也许有另一种解释。他说，如果成瘾和你的化学钩子无关呢？

cues.en: What if addiction is about your cage?
cues.zh: 如果成瘾和你的笼子有关呢？

cues.en: What if addiction is an adaptation to your environment? Looking at this, there was another professor called Peter Cohen in The Netherlands who said, maybe we shouldn't even call it addiction.
cues.zh: 如果成瘾是对你所处环境的一种适应呢？看到这些，荷兰还有一位教授叫Peter Cohen，他说，也许我们根本不该叫它成瘾。

cues.en: Maybe we should call it bonding.
cues.zh: 也许我们应该叫它建立联结。

cues.en: Human beings have a natural and innate need to bond. When we're happy and healthy, we'll bond and connect with each other.
cues.zh: 人类有一种与生俱来的联结需求。当我们快乐健康时，我们会彼此建立联结和联系。

cues.en: But if you can't do that
cues.zh: 但如果你做不到

cues.en: because you're traumatized or isolated or beaten down by life, you will bond with something that will give you some sense of relief. Now, that might be gambling, that might be pornography,
cues.zh: 因为你受过创伤，或被孤立，或被生活压垮，你就会依附于某种能给你带来解脱感的东西。那可能是赌博，可能是色情，

cues.en: that might be cocaine,
cues.zh: 可能是可卡因，

cues.en: that might be cannabis,
cues.zh: 可能是大麻，

cues.en: but you will bond and connect with something because that's our nature.
cues.zh: 但你会依附并联系上某种东西，因为这是我们的天性。

cues.en: That's what we want as human beings. And I think, you know, at first I found this quite a difficult thing to get my head around, but one way to help me to think about it is... And I can see, you know, I've got over by my seat there a bottle of water. Right? I'm looking at lots of you, and lots of you have bottles of water with you. Right?
cues.zh: 这就是我们作为人类想要的。我觉得，一开始我发现这件事很难理解，但帮助我思考它的一个方式是……你看，我座位旁边有一瓶水。对吧？我看着你们很多人，你们很多人都带着水瓶。对吧？

cues.en: Forget drugs, forget the drug war. Totally legally, all of those bottles of water
cues.zh: 忘掉毒品，忘掉毒品战争。完全合法地，所有这些水瓶

cues.en: could be bottles of vodka. Right? We could all be getting drunk, I might, after this.
cues.zh: 都可以是伏特加瓶。对吧？我们都可以喝醉，我说不定讲完就喝。

cues.en: But we're not. Right? Now, because you've been able to afford the approximately gazillion pounds that it costs to get into a TED Talk, I'm guessing you guys could afford to be drinking vodka for the next six months. You wouldn't end up homeless.
cues.zh: 但我们没有。对吧？因为你们能付得起参加TED演讲大约天文数字的英镑，我猜你们这些人负担得起接下来六个月都喝伏特加。你们不会沦落街头。

cues.en: You're not going to do that. And the reason you're not going to do that
cues.zh: 你们不会那么做。而你们不会那么做的原因

cues.en: is not because anyone's stopping you. It's because you've got bonds and connections that you want to be present for. You've got work you love, you've got people you love, you've got healthy relationships.
cues.zh: 不是因为有人在阻止你们。而是因为你们有想要在场守护的羁绊和联系。你们有热爱的工作，有爱的人，有健康的关系。

cues.en: And a core part of addiction I came to think, and I believe the evidence suggests, is about not being able to bear to be present in your life. Now,
cues.zh: 我认为成瘾的核心部分，而且我相信证据也表明，就是无法忍受活在当下。现在，

cues.en: this has really significant implications. The most obvious implications are for the war on drugs. Right?
cues.zh: 这有着非常重大的意义。最明显的影响是针对禁毒战争的。对吧？

cues.en: In Arizona,
cues.zh: 在亚利桑那州，

cues.en: I went out with a group of women
cues.zh: 我和一群女性一起外出，

cues.en: who were made to wear t shirts saying, was a drug addict, and go out on chain gangs and dig graves while members of the public could jeer at them.
cues.zh: 她们被迫穿上写着“曾是吸毒者”的T恤，出去参加锁链队挖坟墓，而公众可以嘲笑她们。

cues.en: And when those women get out of prison, they're going to have criminal records that mean they'll never work in the legal economy again. Now, that's a very extreme example, obviously, in the case of the chain gang, but actually, almost everywhere in the world, we treat addicts to some degree like that. We punish them, we shame them, we give them criminal records, we put barriers between them reconnecting.
cues.zh: 当这些女性出狱后，她们的犯罪记录意味着她们再也无法在合法经济中工作。显然，在锁链队这个案例中，这是一个非常极端的例子，但实际上，世界上几乎所有地方，我们都在某种程度上这样对待成瘾者。我们惩罚他们，羞辱他们，给他们犯罪记录，在他们重新连接的道路上设置障碍。

cues.en: There was a doctor in Canada, Doctor. Gabon Marte, an amazing man who said to me, If you wanted to design a system that would make addiction worse, you would design that system.
cues.zh: 加拿大有一位医生，加博尔·马特医生，一个了不起的人对我说，如果你想设计一个让成瘾更严重的系统，你就会设计出那个系统。

cues.en: Now, there's a place that decided to do the exact opposite, and I went there to see how it worked. In the year 2000, Portugal had one of the worst drug problems in Europe. One percent of the population was addicted to heroin, which is kind of mind blowing. And every year, they tried the American way more and more. They punished people and stigmatized them and shamed them more, and every year, the problem got worse. And one day, the prime minister and the leader of the opposition got together and basically said, look, we can't go on with a country where we're having ever more people becoming heroin addicts. Let's set up a panel of scientists and doctors to figure out
cues.zh: 有一个地方决定做完全相反的事，我去那里看看它是如何运作的。2000年，葡萄牙有着欧洲最严重的毒品问题之一。百分之一的人口对海洛因上瘾，这有点令人震惊。每年，他们越来越多地尝试美国的方式。他们更多地惩罚、污名化和羞辱人们，而每年问题都变得更糟。有一天，总理和反对党领袖聚在一起，基本上说，看，我们不能继续这样下去，一个国家里越来越多的人成为海洛因成瘾者。让我们成立一个科学家和医生小组来弄清楚

cues.en: what would genuinely solve the problem. And this subpanel led by an amazing man called Doctor. Hua Gu Lao to look at all this new evidence,
cues.zh: 什么才能真正解决问题。这个小组由一位名叫华古劳医生的了不起的人领导，研究所有这些新证据，

cues.en: and they came back,
cues.zh: 他们回来了，

cues.en: and they said,
cues.zh: 他们说，

cues.en: decriminalize
cues.zh: 非罪化

cues.en: all drugs,
cues.zh: 所有毒品，

cues.en: from cannabis to crack.
cues.zh: 从大麻到快克。

cues.en: But, and this is the crucial next step, take all the money we used to spend on cutting addicts off, on disconnecting them, and spend it instead on reconnecting them with the society.
cues.zh: 但关键的下一步是，把过去用来切断成瘾者、让他们与社会脱节的所有资金，转而用于帮助他们重新融入社会。

cues.en: And that's not really what we think of. What they did wasn't really what we think of as drug treatment in The United States and Britain. So they do do residential rehab, they do do psychological therapy that does have some value, but the biggest thing they did was the complete opposite of what we do, a massive program of job creation for addicts and microloans for addicts to set up small businesses. So say you used to be a mechanic. When you're ready, they go to a garage, and they'll say, if you employ this guy for a year, we'll pay half his wages. The goal was to make sure that every addict in Portugal had something to get out of bed for in the morning. And when I went and met the addicts in Portugal, was fascinating. What they said is, as they rediscovered purpose,
cues.zh: 而这并不是我们通常所想的那样。他们所做的，跟美国人和英国人所认为的戒毒治疗并不一样。他们确实有住院康复，确实有心理治疗，那些有一定价值，但他们做的最重要的事情跟我们完全相反——一个庞大的项目，为成瘾者创造就业，并提供小额贷款让他们创业。比方说你以前是机械师，等你准备好了，他们就去一家修车厂说，如果你雇这个人一年，我们付他一半工资。目标是确保葡萄牙每个成瘾者早上都有起床的理由。我去葡萄牙见那些成瘾者时，觉得特别有意思。他们说，随着他们重新找到目标，

cues.en: they rediscovered bonds and relationships with the wider society.
cues.zh: 他们也重新找到了与更广泛社会的联系和关系。

cues.en: It'll be fifteen years this year since that experiment began,
cues.zh: 到今年，那个实验已经开始了十五年，

cues.en: and the results are in.
cues.zh: 结果出来了。

cues.en: Injecting drug use is down in Portugal, according to the British Journal of Criminology,
cues.zh: 据《英国犯罪学杂志》报道，葡萄牙的注射吸毒下降了

cues.en: Overdose is massively down, HIV is massively down among addicts.
cues.zh: 过量吸毒大幅下降，成瘾者中的HIV也大幅下降。

cues.en: Addiction in every study is significantly down. One of the ways you know it's worked so well is that almost nobody in Portugal wants to go back to the old system.
cues.zh: 每项研究中，成瘾率都显著下降。你知道它效果有多好的一个标志是，葡萄牙几乎没人想回到旧制度。

cues.en: Now, that's the political
cues.zh: 这就是政治

cues.en: implications. I actually think there's a layer of implications to all this research below that. You know, we live in a culture where people feel really increasingly vulnerable to all sorts of addictions, whether it's to their smartphones
cues.zh: 影响。其实我觉得，所有这些研究下面还有一层影响。你知道，我们生活在一个文化里，人们越来越觉得自己对各种各样的上瘾都无能为力，不管是智能手机

cues.en: or to shopping or to eating. You know, before these talks began, you guys know this, that we were told we weren't allowed to have our smartphones on, and I have to say, a lot of you looked an awful lot like addicts who were being told their dealer was going be unavailable for the next couple of hours. And a lot of us feel like that, and it might sound weird to say, oh, you know, I've been talking about how disconnection is a major driver of addiction, but weird to say it's growing because you think, well, we're the most connected society there's ever been, surely. But I increasingly began to think that the connection we have, the connections we have, we think we have, are like a kind of parody of human connection. If you have a crisis in your life, you'll notice something.
cues.zh: 购物还是吃东西。你们知道，在这些演讲开始之前，我们被告知不许开智能手机，我得说，你们很多人看起来特别像瘾君子，被告知他们的毒贩接下来几个小时都联系不上了。我们很多人都这么觉得，说起来可能有点怪，我一直在讲断连是上瘾的主要驱动因素，但说它在加剧听起来挺怪的，因为你会想，我们明明是有史以来连接最紧密的社会，肯定的啊。但我越来越觉得，我们拥有的连接，我们以为拥有的连接，像是对人类连接的一种戏仿。如果你生活中遇到危机，你会注意到一件事。

cues.en: It won't be your Twitter followers who come to sit with you. It won't be your Facebook friends who help you turn it around. It'll be your flesh and blood friends who you have deep and nuanced and textured face to face relationships with. And I think... There's a there's a study I learned about from Bill McKibben, the environmental writer, I think tells us a lot about this. It looked at the number of close friends the average American believes they can call on in a crisis.
cues.zh: 来陪你坐着的不会是你的Twitter粉丝。帮你扭转局面的不会是你的Facebook好友。而是那些跟你有着深入、细腻、有质感的面对面关系的血肉之交。而且我觉得……我从环境作家Bill McKibben那里了解到一项研究，我觉得很能说明问题。它考察了普通美国人认为自己在危机中能求助的密友数量。

cues.en: That number has been declining steadily since the nineteen fifties.
cues.zh: 这个数字从五十年代以来一直在稳步下降。

cues.en: The amount of floor space an individual has in their home has been steadily increasing,
cues.zh: 而个人家中的居住面积却一直在稳步增加，

cues.en: I think that's like a metaphor
cues.zh: 我觉得这像是一个隐喻

cues.en: for the choice we've made as a culture. Right? We've traded floor space for friends, we've traded stuff for connections, and the result is that we are one of the loneliest societies there has ever been. Bruce Alexander, the guy who did the Rat Park experiment, says, we talk all the time in addiction
cues.zh: 代表我们作为一种文化所做的选择。对吧？我们用居住面积换来了朋友，用物质换来了人际关系，结果就是我们成了有史以来最孤独的社会之一。做老鼠公园实验的布鲁斯·亚历山大说，我们在成瘾问题上一直在谈

cues.en: about individual recovery, and it's right to talk about that. But we need to talk much more about social recovery.
cues.zh: 个人康复，谈这个是对的。但我们需要更多地谈论社会康复。

cues.en: Something's gone wrong with us, not just as individuals, but as a group. And we've created a society where, for a lot of us, life looks a whole lot more like that isolated cage and a whole lot less like Rat Park.
cues.zh: 我们出了问题，不只是作为个体，而是作为一个群体。我们创造了一个社会，对很多人来说，生活更像那个孤立的笼子，而不太像老鼠公园。

cues.en: If I'm honest,
cues.zh: 说实话，

cues.en: this isn't why I went into it. Right? I didn't go in to discover the political stuff, the social stuff. I wanted to know how to help the people I love. And when I came back from this long journey and I'd learned all this,
cues.zh: 这不是我进入这个领域的原因。对吧？我不是为了发现政治问题、社会问题。我想知道怎么帮助我爱的人。当我结束这段漫长的旅程，学到了这一切之后，

cues.en: I looked at the addicts in my life, and if, you know, if you're really candid,
cues.zh: 我看着生活中的成瘾者，如果你真的很坦诚的话，

cues.en: it's hard loving an addict, there's going be lots of people who know in this room you're angry a lot of the time.
cues.zh: 爱一个成瘾者很难，这个房间里有很多人都知道，你很多时候是愤怒的。

cues.en: And I think one of the reasons why this debate is so charged
cues.zh: 我觉得这场争论之所以如此激烈

cues.en: is because it runs through the heart of each of us. Right? Everyone has a bit of them that looks at an addict and thinks, I wish someone would just stop you. And the kind of script we're told for how to deal with the addicts in our lives is typified by, I think, by the reality show Intervention. If you guys haven't seen it, I think everything in our lives is typified by reality TV, but that's another TED
cues.zh: 是因为它贯穿了我们每个人的内心。对吧？每个人心里都有一点，看着一个成瘾者想，我真希望有人能让你停下来。而我们被告知的处理生活中成瘾者的剧本，我觉得典型代表就是真人秀《干预》。如果你们没看过，我觉得我们生活中的一切都被真人秀代表了，但那是另一个TED

cues.en: talk.
cues.zh: 演讲了。

cues.en: If you've never seen the show Intervention, it's a pretty simple premise. You get an addict, all the people in their life, gather them together and confront
cues.zh: 如果你没看过《干预》这个节目，它的设定很简单。你有一个成瘾者，把他生活里所有的人聚在一起，和他们当面对质

cues.en: them with what they're doing, and they say, if you don't shape up, we're going to cut you off. Right? So what they do is they take the connection to the addict and they threaten it. They make it contingent on the addict behaving the way they want.
cues.zh: 他们在做什么，然后他们说，如果你不改，我们就要跟你断绝关系。对吧？所以他们做的，就是拿走跟成瘾者之间的连接，以此威胁。他们让这段关系取决于成瘾者是否按他们想要的方式行事。

cues.en: And I see began why that approach doesn't work, and I began to think that almost that's like the importing
cues.zh: 我开始明白为什么那种方式行不通，我也开始觉得，那几乎就是把

cues.en: of the logic of the drug war into our private lives.
cues.zh: 毒品战争的逻辑搬进了我们的私人生活。

cues.en: So I was thinking, well, how can I be Portuguese?
cues.zh: 于是我想，好吧，我怎样才能做那个葡萄牙人？

cues.en: Right? And what I try to do now, and I can't tell you I do it consistently and I can't tell you it's easy,
cues.zh: 对吧？我现在试着做的——我没法说我一直都做得到，也没法说这很容易——

cues.en: is to say to the addicts in my life that I want to deepen the connection with them, to say to them, I love you whether you're using or you're not. I love you, whatever state you're in, and if you need me, I'll come and sit with you, because I love you, and I don't want you to be alone or to feel alone.
cues.zh: 就是对我生活里的成瘾者说，我想加深和他们的连接，对他们说：不管你用不用，我都爱你。不管你处在什么状态，我都爱你，如果你需要我，我会来陪你坐坐，因为我爱你，我不想让你孤身一人，也不想让你感到孤单。

cues.en: And I think the core of that message,
cues.zh: 而我认为这条信息的核心，

cues.en: you're not alone, we love you, has to be at every level of how we respond to addicts, socially, politically and individually.
cues.zh: “你并不孤单，我们爱你”，必须体现在我们回应成瘾者的每一个层面——社会的、政治的、个人的。

cues.en: For a hundred years now,
cues.zh: 一百年来，

cues.en: we've been singing war songs about addicts.
cues.zh: 我们一直在唱关于成瘾者的战歌。

cues.en: I think all along, we should have been singing love songs to them, because the opposite of addiction is not sobriety.
cues.zh: 我觉得一直以来，我们本该对他们唱的是情歌，因为成瘾的反面并不是清醒。

cues.en: The opposite of addiction
cues.zh: 成瘾的反面

cues.en: is connection.
cues.zh: 是连接。

cues.en: Thank you.
cues.zh: 谢谢。

cues.en: Thank you.
cues.zh: 谢谢。
